title: Why Silver Medalists Look Less Happy
text:
In the mid-1990s Victoria Husted Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University studied television footage of athletes at the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona. They showed clips of silver and bronze medalists, captured at the moment the athletes learned their result and later on the medal stand, to students who knew little about sports and did not know who had placed where.

The students rated each athlete's expression on a scale from agony to ecstasy. On average, the bronze medalists looked happier than the silver medalists, both right after the competition and on the podium. In another part of the study, the researchers analyzed televised interviews and found that silver medalists talked more about what they had almost achieved, while bronze medalists talked more about having at least made it.

The explanation lay in what the athletes compared themselves with. The silver medalist, just short of first place, naturally thinks of the gold that slipped away. The bronze medalist, just above fourth place, thinks of how close they came to going home with nothing. The objectively better result produced the worse feeling.

The authors linked this to counterfactual thinking: our feelings about an outcome depend heavily on the alternatives that come to mind. A follow-up study of athletes at a regional athletic competition in New York found the same pattern.
lesson: How you feel about a result depends on what you compare it with. When you catch yourself dwelling on what you just missed, also consider what you just avoided.
people: Victoria Husted Medvec, Scott Madey, Thomas Gilovich
location: Cornell University, Ithaca, USA (footage of the 1992 Barcelona Olympics)
source: Medvec, V. H., Madey, S. F., and Gilovich, T. (1995). When less is more: Counterfactual thinking and satisfaction among Olympic medalists. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(4), 603-610.
caveat: Later work (McGraw, Mellers and Tetlock, 2005) found that athletes' prior expectations also shape their reactions, so the pattern does not always hold.
